title: The narrowest exception in company law
subtitle: Piercing the corporate veil after Prest
objectives: State the narrow 'evasion principle' set out in Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd, and distinguish it from the looser 'piercing the veil' language used in older cases

Distinguish concealment (where the company merely hides the true facts) from evasion (where the company is interposed to defeat an existing legal obligation) as the dividing line for when courts will disregard personality
Apply the evasion principle to a new fact pattern, correctly rejecting agency and 'single economic unit' arguments as independent routes to piercing the veil

leadingAuthorities.citation: Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd [2013] UKSC 34
leadingAuthorities.role: Narrows veil-piercing to a true 'evasion principle': the veil may be pierced only where a defendant deliberately uses a company to evade an existing legal obligation or frustrate its enforcement

leadingAuthorities.citation: Adams v Cape Industries plc [1990] Ch 433
leadingAuthorities.role: Rejects 'single economic unit' membership of a corporate group, by itself, as a ground for piercing the veil

leadingAuthorities.citation: VTB Capital plc v Nutritek International Corp [2013] UKSC 5
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms piercing is a remedy of last resort that cannot be used to impose contractual liability on a non-party controller, and rejects agency as a free-standing piercing route

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Students often arrive at this lesson expecting a flexible, fact-sensitive 'fairness' doctrine, because that's how older cases and textbooks sometimes describe it. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the case names — this lesson checks whether you can tell a genuine evasion case from the many scenarios that look like one but aren't.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans towards scenario questions that look like veil-piercing but usually aren't — read each fact pattern for whether an existing obligation is being deliberately evaded.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and take it slowly — Prest reset the vocabulary this whole area uses, and the rest of the lesson assumes you can state the evasion principle precisely, not just gesture at 'piercing the veil'.

overview.hook: For decades, 'piercing the corporate veil' was one of the vaguest phrases in English law — invoked whenever a judge thought the corporate form was being used unfairly, with no settled test for when. In 2013 the Supreme Court in Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd tried to end the vagueness for good, replacing loose talk of 'piercing' with a single, narrow question: is the defendant using a company to evade an obligation they already owe? Most students still answer exam questions as though the old, looser doctrine survived. It didn't — and this lesson is about the much narrower gate that replaced it.
overview.lawStatedNotice: The evasion principle from Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd [2013] UKSC 34 is settled Supreme Court authority and has not been overturned. Some academic commentary continues to debate the precise boundary between the 'concealment' and 'evasion' categories in edge cases, and lower courts occasionally still use looser 'piercing' language drawn from pre-Prest authority — this lesson teaches the Prest framework as the current, controlling test. Law stated as at 23 September 2026.

parts.heading: A divorce case that rewrote a doctrine
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Michael Prest was a wealthy businessman whose marriage to Yasmin Prest ended in divorce. Several valuable London properties, though occupied by the family and treated as his throughout the marriage, were held in the names of companies Mr Prest wholly owned and controlled — a common structure in some sectors for tax and commercial reasons. In the financial remedy proceedings, the trial judge ordered the companies to transfer the properties to Mrs Prest, reasoning that Mr Prest so completely controlled the companies that the corporate veil should be pierced and their property treated as his.

The Court of Appeal disagreed, and the case reached the Supreme Court on a question that turned out to matter far beyond family law: on what principled basis, if any, can a court treat a company's assets as belonging to the individual who controls it? The loose, decades-old language of 'piercing the veil where justice requires it' had never been reduced to a workable test, and Lord Sumption's leading judgment set out to fix that.

The Supreme Court held that the properties should indeed be transferred to Mrs Prest — but not by piercing the veil at all. It found, on the facts, that the companies held the properties on resulting trust for Mr Prest because of how they had originally been funded and acquired — an ordinary property-law route available regardless of the corporate structure. Genuine veil-piercing, the Court held, was not made out on these facts, and in the course of saying so it narrowed the doctrine dramatically for every future case.

components.factsShort: In divorce proceedings, a wife sought to have London properties held by her husband's wholly-owned companies transferred to her as part of the financial settlement.
components.ratioShort: The corporate veil can be pierced only where a person is under an existing legal obligation which they deliberately evade, or whose enforcement they deliberately frustrate, by interposing a company they control — the 'evasion principle'.

expanded.facts: Michael Prest wholly owned and controlled a group of companies that held title to several valuable properties used by his family. On divorce, his wife Yasmin sought a transfer of those properties as part of the financial remedy award. The trial judge pierced the corporate veil on the basis of Mr Prest's complete control; the Court of Appeal reversed.
expanded.judgmentExtract: Lord Sumption held that 'piercing the corporate veil' should be confined to a narrow evasion principle: it applies only where a person is under an existing legal obligation or liability, or subject to an existing legal restriction, which they deliberately evade or whose enforcement they deliberately frustrate by interposing a company under their control. Where a company is merely used to conceal the true facts — who really owns an asset, or who is really a party to a transaction — the court does not need to pierce anything; it simply looks behind the concealment to find the truth, using ordinary evidential and legal principles that apply regardless of the corporate form.
expanded.significance: Prest is now the leading and controlling statement of when English courts will disregard separate legal personality. It replaces decades of inconsistent 'piercing' language with a single, narrow test, and — just as importantly — shows that many cases that look like veil-piercing problems are actually solved by ordinary legal doctrines (here, resulting trusts) that never required touching the veil at all.

interaction.prompt: Did the Supreme Court in Prest ultimately transfer the properties to Mrs Prest by piercing the corporate veil?
options: No — it found the companies held the properties on resulting trust for Mr Prest, a route that did not require piercing the veil
Yes — it pierced the veil because Mr Prest controlled the companies completely
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right, and this is the detail students most often miss: the actual outcome in Prest rested on a resulting trust, not on veil-piercing — the veil-piercing discussion is significant for narrowing the doctrine, not for deciding the case.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at how the case was actually decided. The properties were transferred because of a resulting trust arising from how they were acquired — the Supreme Court expressly held that veil-piercing was not made out on these facts.

parts.heading: Concealment and evasion: the line that matters
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Lord Sumption's judgment in Prest turns on a distinction that is easy to state and genuinely easy to misapply under exam pressure: concealment versus evasion. Only evasion is 'piercing the veil' in the strict sense; concealment is not piercing at all, because nothing about the company's separate personality needs to be disregarded to reach the answer.

Concealment describes cases where a company is interposed so that the real actors or the real facts are hidden behind it — but the underlying legal analysis doesn't actually require ignoring the company. The court simply looks behind the facade to find out who is really doing what, using ordinary rules of evidence, agency, trusts or contract, exactly as it would for a concealment device that wasn't corporate at all. No special veil-piercing doctrine is needed, because the company's separate personality was never really the obstacle.

Evasion is the narrow category the doctrine now actually governs: a defendant is already under a specific legal obligation or liability — a contractual duty, a statutory restriction, a court order — and deliberately interposes a company they control specifically to evade that obligation or frustrate its enforcement. Only here does 'piercing the veil' do genuine work, because the whole point is to stop separate personality from being used as a shield against a liability that already, independently, exists.

components.label: Concealment vs evasion
points: Concealment: the company hides the true facts, but the legal analysis doesn't require disregarding personality — the court simply finds the truth using ordinary principles
Evasion: the defendant already owes a specific legal obligation and interposes a company specifically to evade it or frustrate its enforcement
Only evasion is 'piercing the veil' properly so called, after Prest
Most fact patterns that look like veil-piercing problems on first read turn out to be concealment cases, resolvable without touching the doctrine at all

components.definition: The narrow post-Prest test for piercing the corporate veil: a court may disregard a company's separate personality only where a person under an existing legal obligation, liability or restriction deliberately interposes a company under their control to evade it or frustrate its enforcement.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is a concealment case rather than a genuine evasion case?
interaction.scenarioA: A defendant, mid-litigation on a debt he already owes, transfers his personal assets into a newly formed company he controls, specifically to put them beyond the claimant's reach.
interaction.scenarioB: A landlord discovers that the 'tenant company' named on a lease was, from the outset, simply a vehicle the true occupier used to sign documents — the court needs only to identify who the real contracting party actually was.
interaction.explanation: B is concealment: the company was used to obscure who the real party was, but establishing that requires no piercing — ordinary contractual and evidential analysis identifies the true party. A is evasion: an existing obligation (the debt) is being deliberately placed beyond reach by interposing a company, which is exactly what the narrow post-Prest doctrine targets.

parts.heading: Groups of companies are not one company
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Before Prest, one of the most persistent arguments for piercing the veil was the 'single economic unit' argument: where a group of companies operates as one integrated business, shouldn't the law treat the group as a single entity, at least for the purpose of making the parent liable for a subsidiary's debts? Adams v Cape Industries plc is the case that killed this argument, decades before Prest confirmed the narrower approach generally.

Cape Industries plc, an English company, had US subsidiaries involved in asbestos mining and marketing. Employees and others injured by asbestos exposure obtained large default judgments against the US subsidiaries in American courts, then tried to enforce those judgments against the English parent company in England — arguing that the corporate group operated as a single economic unit, so the parent should answer for the group's liabilities.

The Court of Appeal firmly rejected this. Each company in a group, the Court held, is a separate legal person with its own separate assets and liabilities, and that remains true even where the group operates as an integrated business under common management. The fact that a corporate structure was deliberately designed, entirely lawfully, so that liabilities arising in one jurisdiction stayed with the subsidiary operating there — rather than exposing the parent's assets — was not, by itself, a basis for piercing anything. A group structure used for perfectly ordinary reasons is not evasion.

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often argue that because several companies in a group are 'really' controlled by the same parent and run as one business, the parent should automatically be liable for a subsidiary's debts.
components.whyItsWrong: Adams v Cape rejects 'single economic unit' as a free-standing ground for piercing. Common ownership, shared management and integrated operations are exactly what a corporate group is — none of that, on its own, amounts to evading an existing obligation. Something more specific — an actual evasion of a specific liability the parent already owed, deliberately routed through a subsidiary — would be needed, and mere group structure is not that.

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact in this scenario that shows the single economic unit argument, alone, will not justify piercing the veil.
interaction.scenarioText: A UK parent company owns 100% of an overseas manufacturing subsidiary, sets its production targets, and consolidates its accounts into the group's annual report. The subsidiary later becomes insolvent owing money to local suppliers, who try to claim against the UK parent purely on the basis that the group operated as one integrated business.
tappableSpans: owns 100% of an overseas manufacturing subsidiary
consolidates its accounts into the group's annual report
purely on the basis that the group operated as one integrated business
interaction.correctSpan: purely on the basis that the group operated as one integrated business
interaction.feedbackCorrect: That's the Adams v Cape point exactly: integrated group operation, common ownership and shared management are ordinary features of a corporate group, not evidence of evasion — the suppliers need something more specific to reach the parent.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look for the phrase that names the single economic unit argument itself, rather than the ordinary facts of group ownership and control that Adams v Cape holds are not enough on their own.

parts.heading: Piercing is not a shortcut to a better defendant
parts.voice: argumentative — states the strongest case for the rule, then complicates it
body: A claimant who has struck a bad bargain, or sued the wrong party, sometimes reaches for veil-piercing as a way of adding a wealthier, better-placed defendant to the claim after the fact. VTB Capital plc v Nutritek International Corp closes that door decisively.

VTB, a bank, had been induced to enter a loan facility by misrepresentations it said were made by individuals behind a company, Nutritek, that was the actual counterparty to the facility agreement. VTB wanted to sue those individuals not just in tort for the misrepresentations, but also in contract, as if they had personally been parties to the loan agreement — effectively asking the court to pierce the veil to attach contractual liability to non-parties who controlled the corporate contracting party.

The Supreme Court refused. Piercing the veil, it held, is a remedy of last resort, available only where no other cause of action will provide an effective remedy — and even where it is available in principle, it cannot be used offensively to create a new liability, such as contractual liability under an agreement the defendant never signed. VTB already had a tort claim available against the individuals for the alleged misrepresentations; there was no gap in the law that veil-piercing needed to fill, and 'agency' or 'control' arguments, without more, do not justify treating a controller as a contracting party.

components.label: What VTB Capital confirms
points: Veil-piercing is a remedy of last resort — it is not available where another adequate cause of action (here, tort for misrepresentation) already exists
Piercing cannot be used offensively to impose a new liability, such as contractual liability, on a non-party controller
Mere control of a company, without a specific act of evasion of an existing obligation, does not justify piercing — echoing and reinforcing the approach later confirmed in Prest
Agency arguments (treating the company as the controller's agent) are analytically separate from veil-piercing and must be established on their own terms, not smuggled in as a piercing shortcut

interaction.prompt: In VTB Capital, why did the Supreme Court refuse to pierce the veil to make the individual controllers personally liable in contract?
options: Because the controllers had no connection to the transaction at all
Because VTB already had an available claim in tort, and piercing cannot be used offensively to create a new contractual liability against a non-party
Because piercing the veil is never available in commercial disputes, only in family cases
interaction.trapExplanation: The tempting wrong answers overstate the rule either way — claiming the controllers had no link to the facts (they did; that was the whole complaint) or claiming piercing never applies in commercial cases (Prest itself confirms it can, narrowly). The actual reasoning is precise: piercing is a last resort, unavailable where another remedy exists, and it cannot manufacture new liabilities against non-parties.

parts.heading: Why the gate is narrow, and staying narrow
parts.voice: reflective — closes the lesson by justifying its own place in the syllabus
body: Step back and the three cases in this lesson tell one consistent story. Prest confines piercing to deliberate evasion of an existing obligation. Adams v Cape refuses to let ordinary group structure count as evasion. VTB Capital refuses to let piercing manufacture a new cause of action where none exists. Each case closes a door that pre-Prest commentary had left ajar.

The policy reason threads through all three: separate legal personality, established in Lesson 1's Salomon, is the foundation the entire corporate form rests on. If courts pierced the veil whenever it felt fair on the facts, that foundation would become unpredictable — businesses, lenders and counterparties structure their affairs on the assumption that a company's liabilities stay with the company. A doctrine kept genuinely narrow protects that predictability, while still leaving a real (if rare) remedy for the specific case of deliberate evasion.

For exam purposes, treat 'piercing the veil' as a near-automatic wrong turn in a problem answer unless the facts show a defendant already under a specific, identifiable legal obligation who has interposed a company specifically to dodge it. In almost every other fact pattern — group structures, hidden ownership, controllers acting through a company — the better answer lies in identifying the true party through ordinary principles, exactly as Prest itself did.

components.title: Deciding whether the veil can be pierced
components.description: The post-Prest decision path for a veil-piercing problem question.

nodes.label: Is the company being used to hide who the real party or real facts are?
Yes → concealment: find the truth using ordinary principles, no piercing needed
No → does the defendant already owe a specific legal obligation?
No existing obligation → piercing unavailable, whatever the group structure or control
Yes → was a company deliberately interposed to evade that obligation or frustrate its enforcement?
Yes → evasion principle may justify piercing (Prest)
No deliberate evasion → piercing unavailable; consider agency, trusts or tort instead

components.textAlternative: To analyse a veil-piercing problem: first ask if the company is being used merely to hide who the real party or facts are — if so, this is concealment, resolved with ordinary principles and no piercing. If not, ask whether the defendant already owes a specific legal obligation — if not, piercing is unavailable regardless of group structure or control (Adams v Cape). If an obligation exists, ask whether a company was deliberately interposed to evade it or frustrate its enforcement — only if so does the evasion principle from Prest potentially justify piercing; otherwise, look to agency, trusts or tort instead (VTB Capital).

interaction.prompt: How confident are you that a claimant can pierce the veil purely because a defendant tightly controls a company and benefits from its assets?
sliderLabels: Confident — control and benefit are enough
Not confident — an existing obligation deliberately evaded is required
interaction.correctPosition: Not confident — an existing obligation deliberately evaded is required
interaction.explanation: Correct to be unconfident. Prest, Adams v Cape and VTB Capital all reject control or benefit alone as sufficient — the evasion principle requires a specific, existing legal obligation that the defendant is deliberately using the company to dodge.

testPool.prompt: State the evasion principle set out in Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd.
acceptableAnswers: a company may be disregarded where used to evade an existing legal obligation
the veil can be pierced only where a person interposes a company to evade an obligation they already owe
testPool.modelAnswer: The corporate veil may be pierced only where a person under an existing legal obligation, liability or restriction deliberately interposes a company under their control to evade it or frustrate its enforcement.

testPool.prompt: Did the Supreme Court in Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd find that genuine veil-piercing was made out on the facts?
options: No — the outcome rested on a resulting trust instead
Yes — the veil was pierced because Mr Prest controlled the companies

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT, by itself, sufficient to justify piercing the corporate veil after Prest?
options: Deliberately transferring assets into a company you control specifically to defeat an existing judgment debt
Owning and completely controlling a company
Both are sufficient on their own
testPool.trapExplanation: Mere ownership and control — however complete — is exactly what Salomon and Prest both confirm is not enough. Only the first option describes deliberate evasion of an existing obligation, which is the narrow ground Prest actually requires.

testPool.prompt: Order the analytical steps a court takes under the post-Prest framework when a veil-piercing argument is raised.
items: Ask whether the company is merely being used to conceal the true facts or parties
If not concealment, ask whether the defendant already owes a specific legal obligation
If an obligation exists, ask whether a company was deliberately interposed to evade it
Pierce the veil only if deliberate evasion of that existing obligation is established

testPool.prompt: Which Act of Parliament sets out the statutory test for when a court may pierce the corporate veil?
options: Companies Act 2006, s 33
There is no statutory test — piercing the veil is a common-law doctrine, developed through cases such as Prest
Insolvency Act 1986, s 214
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Correct. Unlike, say, wrongful trading (a statutory creature of the Insolvency Act 1986), veil-piercing has never been codified — its content is entirely a matter of case law, currently governed by Prest.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: This is a case-law doctrine, not a statutory one. No Act of Parliament sets out a test for piercing the veil; the governing test comes from Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd and the cases leading up to it.

testPool.prompt: In the extract below, highlight the sentence that states the evasion principle from Prest.
testPool.passage: The court may be justified in disregarding the corporate veil if there is a legal right against the person in control of it which exists independently of the company's involvement, and a company is interposed so that the separate legal personality of the company will defeat the right or frustrate its enforcement. It is the evasion of that existing right, not mere control, which justifies piercing.
testPool.ratioSentence: It is the evasion of that existing right, not mere control, which justifies piercing.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that most clearly points towards deliberate evasion, rather than mere concealment or ordinary group structure.
testPool.scenarioText: Days after losing an arbitration award requiring him to pay £2 million, Karim transfers his only substantial UK asset — a commercial building — into a newly formed company he alone owns, for no consideration, specifically so the award creditor cannot enforce against it.
tappableSpans: Days after losing an arbitration award
transfers his only substantial UK asset
a newly formed company he alone owns
specifically so the award creditor cannot enforce against it
testPool.correctSpan: specifically so the award creditor cannot enforce against it
testPool.explanation: This phrase supplies the deliberate-evasion element Prest requires: an existing obligation (the arbitration award) and a company interposed specifically to frustrate its enforcement. The other facts describe the mechanism, but this is the evasive purpose the doctrine actually turns on.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario is closer to Adams v Cape Industries than to Prest?
testPool.scenarioA: A UK parent company and its foreign subsidiary are run as one integrated business under shared management, and a claimant wants the parent liable purely because of that integration, with no separate obligation owed by the parent.
testPool.scenarioB: An individual, already bound by a non-compete clause in a settlement agreement, sets up a new company through which he immediately starts the exact competing business the clause prohibits.
testPool.explanation: A mirrors Adams v Cape: integrated group operation and common management, without more, is not evasion. B mirrors Prest: an existing obligation (the non-compete) is being deliberately routed around using a company — the paradigm evasion case.

testPool.prompt: A claimant sues a company for breach of contract and, when the company turns out to have no assets, seeks to make the sole director personally liable purely on the ground that the director controlled the company and benefited from the contract. No existing obligation was owed by the director before the contract was made. Applying Prest, does this argument succeed?
options: No — control and incidental benefit are not evasion of a pre-existing obligation, which the evasion principle requires
Yes — any director who benefits from a company's contract can be made personally liable on it
Yes — because the company has no assets, the veil is automatically pierced to reach the director
testPool.explanation: There is no pre-existing obligation here that the director is evading — the contract itself created the only relevant obligation, and it was the company's, not the director's. Prest requires an obligation that already existed independently of the company's involvement; a company simply lacking assets is not evasion.

testPool.prompt: In VTB Capital, was piercing the veil available to impose contractual liability on individuals who were never parties to the contract?
options: No — the Supreme Court held piercing cannot be used to manufacture new contractual liability against a non-party
Yes — because the individuals controlled the contracting company

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that a court will pierce the veil whenever no other remedy is available and the claimant's case seems fair on the facts?
sliderLabels: Not confident — an existing obligation deliberately evaded is still required, even as a last resort
testPool.correctPosition: Not confident — an existing obligation deliberately evaded is still required, even as a last resort
testPool.explanation: Not confident is right. VTB Capital confirms piercing is a remedy of last resort — meaning it is only available where nothing else works — but 'last resort' describes when it might be used, not a relaxation of what must be shown: deliberate evasion of an existing obligation is still required.

testPool.prompt: Beatrice owes a substantial debt under a personal guarantee she signed for a friend's failed business loan. Shortly after the lender demands payment, Beatrice incorporates a new company, transfers her freelance consultancy income and her only valuable asset (a flat) into it, and continues working exactly as before, now invoiced through the company. The lender wants to enforce the guarantee debt against the company's assets. Analyse whether the veil can be pierced.
factsToOrder: Beatrice owes an existing debt under a personal guarantee
The lender demands payment shortly before she incorporates
She transfers her income and only valuable asset into the new company
She continues working exactly as before, now invoiced through the company
The lender seeks to enforce against the company's assets

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether the corporate veil can be pierced to allow the lender to enforce Beatrice's personal guarantee debt against the assets of her newly formed company.
modelAnswer.rule: Under Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd, the veil may be pierced only where a person under an existing legal obligation deliberately interposes a company they control to evade that obligation or frustrate its enforcement.
modelAnswer.application: Beatrice already owed a specific, existing legal obligation (the guarantee debt) before incorporating. The timing — incorporation shortly after the lender's demand — together with transferring her only substantial asset and ongoing income into the company while continuing the same work, points strongly towards a deliberate scheme to place her assets beyond the lender's reach. This is the paradigm evasion scenario the Prest test targets, distinguishable from ordinary, non-evasive reasons for incorporating.
modelAnswer.conclusion: On these facts, the veil is likely to be pierced: the timing and pattern of asset transfer support a finding of deliberate evasion of an existing, specific obligation.

testPool.prompt: A problem question describes a wholly-owned subsidiary used, entirely lawfully and for ordinary tax-planning reasons, to hold a group's overseas property. A creditor of the parent company argues the veil should be pierced because the arrangement 'looks suspicious.' What is the strongest response?
options: The arrangement should be pierced because tax planning through subsidiaries is inherently evasive
'Looking suspicious' is not the test; without an existing obligation the parent is deliberately using the subsidiary to evade, Adams v Cape and Prest both hold this is not evasion
The veil can never be pierced where a subsidiary is involved, regardless of the facts
testPool.trapExplanation: Both wrong options overstate the rule in opposite directions. Lawful, ordinary tax or liability-structuring through subsidiaries is not automatically evasion (that would make almost every corporate group vulnerable); but piercing is also not categorically impossible with subsidiaries (Prest itself concerned wholly-owned companies). The correct answer applies the actual test: an existing obligation, deliberately evaded, is required either way.

testPool.prompt: Name the three cases covered in this lesson and, in one phrase each, what each one rejects or confirms about veil-piercing.
acceptableAnswers: Prest confirms the narrow evasion principle; Adams v Cape rejects single economic unit; VTB Capital rejects piercing as a route to new contractual liability
Prest, Adams v Cape, VTB Capital
testPool.modelAnswer: Prest v Petrodel Resources Ltd confirms the narrow evasion principle; Adams v Cape Industries rejects the single economic unit argument as a ground for piercing; VTB Capital plc v Nutritek confirms piercing is a last-resort remedy that cannot manufacture new contractual liability against a non-party controller.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is reaching for 'piercing the veil' as a general fairness doctrine whenever a controller benefits from a company's separateness. After Prest, the doctrine only bites where a specific, existing legal obligation is being deliberately evaded — everything else (group structures, hidden ownership, disappointed creditors chasing a better-off defendant) is either concealment, agency, trusts, tort, or simply not actionable at all.
